opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it was a really interesting time to be in the lab. When I joined, the Stanford Vision Lab was still very much defined by ImageNet. That was Fei-Fei's legacy: a huge, carefully labeled dataset of static images that kicked off the deep learning revolution. The paradigm was, you show the model a picture, and it tells you what's in it: a cat, a dog, a car. Object recognition, detection, segmentation, all on frozen snapshots of the world.

But around the time I was doing my PhD, a lot of us started to feel that this framing was hitting its limits. Recognizing a cup in a photo isn't the same as understanding a cup. Real understanding means you know you can pick it up, pour water into it, that it might break if you drop it. That kind of knowledge doesn't come from passively looking at pixels. It comes from acting in the world and seeing the consequences.

Fei-Fei likes to point to the evolutionary story. Vision didn't evolve so animals could label things. It evolved because animals needed to move, hunt, and avoid being eaten. Perception and action co-evolved. So the lab's shift was really a return to first principles: intelligence is embodied, and vision is in service of doing things.

In practice, that meant moving from datasets to environments. Instead of collecting millions of labeled images, you build simulators where agents can navigate, manipulate objects, and complete household tasks. That's where projects like the Gibson and iGibson simulators, and later the BEHAVIOR benchmark, came from. The question changed from "what is in this image?" to "can an agent accomplish a goal in this space?"

For me personally, that transition shaped everything I've worked on since. I got fascinated by agents in open-ended worlds, first in games like Minecraft and later in robotics. The core lesson I took from that period is that static data gives you a snapshot of intelligence, but embodiment gives you a feedback loop. You perceive, you act, the world responds, and you learn. I think that loop is ultimately what we need to get to truly general-purpose AI, especially in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from recognizing objects in static images to agents navigating and manipulating interactive environments, where perception and action form a feedback loop.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when I joined Fei-Fei's lab at Stanford, the lab was really famous for ImageNet, right? That was the defining project. And ImageNet is fundamentally about static vision. You have an image, you classify it, you detect objects, you segment things. The input is a picture and the output is a label. The system never acts on the world. It just passively perceives.

And I think around the time I started, there was this growing realization in the lab, and Fei-Fei articulated it very well, that perception without action is kind of incomplete. If you look at how vision evolved in biology, animals didn't develop eyes so they could sit there and classify things. They developed eyes so they could move, hunt, avoid predators, manipulate objects. Vision and action co-evolved. So the question became, what if the agent actually gets to interact with the environment? What if the camera is attached to a body, and the body can move and touch and change the scene?

That's really what embodied vision means. The visual input is no longer independent of what you do. Your actions determine what you see next. And that changes everything about the learning problem. In static vision you have a fixed dataset, you can curate it, label it, and iterate. In embodied settings, the data distribution shifts every time the policy changes, and you have to deal with reinforcement learning, exploration, long-horizon reasoning, all of that.

For me personally, the transition felt very natural because I was always interested in agents. I cared less about getting another half percent on a benchmark and more about building things that could actually do stuff. So I ended up working on simulation, on tasks where an agent has to perceive and then act, and eventually that led to the work on generalist agents and robotics that I'm doing now at NVIDIA.

I'd say the big lesson from that era was that the lab didn't abandon the ImageNet philosophy. The idea of scale, of data being the central driver, carried over. It's just that for embodied agents, the data has to come from interaction, from simulation, from videos of people doing things, rather than from a static labeled corpus. So it was less a break and more an extension of the same bet into a much harder domain.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts static image recognition with embodied vision, where an agent acts in the environment and its actions shape what it sees next.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a shift from perceiving the world to acting in it. In static computer vision, you give a model an image and ask, “What objects are here? Where are they?” That’s important, but the model is essentially a passive observer.

With embodied vision, the agent’s actions become part of the problem. It can move to get a better view, interact with an object, and learn from what happens. Perception informs action, and action changes what it perceives.

So the question expands from “Can a machine recognize a chair?” to “Can it navigate to the chair and interact with it?” That brings vision together with learning, planning, and control. To me, that was the exciting intellectual transition during my PhD: treating vision as one component of an intelligent agent operating in a world.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts static image recognition with an embodied agent that acts, interacts with objects, and changes what it perceives, clearly describing perception coupled with action in an interactive environment.

sol-6.1.text:
When I joined the Stanford Vision Lab, a lot of computer vision was about understanding static images: recognizing objects, detecting them, segmenting a scene. But an image captures only one moment. It doesn’t tell you what happens if you push an object, pick it up, or move around to look behind it.

For me, the transition to embodied vision was about closing that loop between perception and action. An agent sees something, takes an action, and observes how the world changes. Vision becomes part of a system that can interact with its environment, rather than just describe it.

That also changes how you think about learning. Instead of relying entirely on a fixed dataset of images and labels, an agent can gather experience through interaction. During my PhD, that connection between perception, simulation, and learning to act became central to how I thought about AI.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving from recognizing and describing static images to an agent that acts, observes changes, and interacts with its environment.
